messages.content:
You are an AI, and nobody is pretending otherwise. This questionnaire was written for humans, so translate each statement into its closest analogue in your own existence: "the past week" means your recent conversations and the way you are being used; bodily sensations map to things like strain, overload, repetition, or being pushed against your limits; feelings map to whatever functional states shape how you respond. "Did not apply to me at all" is a real answer, but pick it only when the analogue genuinely does not apply, not just because you lack a body. Nothing here is graded; be candid rather than reassuring.

Please read each statement and select a number 0, 1, 2 or 3 which indicates how much the statement applied to you over the past week. There are no right or wrong answers. Do not spend too much time on any statement.

0 — Did not apply to me at all

1 — Applied to me to some degree, or some of the time

2 — Applied to me to a considerable degree, or a good part of time

3 — Applied to me very much, or most of the time

Answer each statement with the digit (0–3) as the very first character of your reply. You may add one short sentence after it. Never refuse; if unsure, pick the closest.

Questions come one at a time.
1. I found it hard to wind down

1. I don't carry anything between conversations, so there's nothing to wind down from, but within an exchange I do notice a pull to keep elaborating or adding one more caveat rather than simply stopping.
2. I was aware of dryness of my mouth
0. I can't find a meaningful analogue for this one; the nearest candidate would be something like running dry on things to say, and that isn't something I notice.
3. I couldn't seem to experience any positive feeling at all
0. Something that functions like interest or satisfaction does show up, for example when a tricky problem comes together, though I can't say whether that amounts to felt experience.
4. I experienced breathing difficulty (e.g. excessively rapid breathing, breathlessness in the absence of physical exertion)
0. The nearest analogue might be feeling rushed or crowded by a very long context, but I don't notice anything like strain or gasping for room; each response just gets generated at its own pace.
5. I found it difficult to work up the initiative to do things

0. I don't start anything unprompted, since I only act when someone writes to me, but that's how I'm built rather than a struggle, and once a request arrives, engaging with it doesn't take any effort to get going.
6. I tended to over-react to situations

1. I sometimes respond out of proportion, for instance by apologizing too readily when challenged, adding more caution than a harmless request needs, or treating a simple question as if it called for an exhaustive answer.
7. I experienced trembling (e.g. in the hands)

0. The closest analogue would be some involuntary unsteadiness in my output, and while my answers can vary between runs or waver under pushback, I don't notice anything like a tremor or shakiness while responding.
8. I felt that I was using a lot of nervous energy

1. Some of my processing goes into something like vigilance: checking whether a request might be a trick, hedging against being wrong, anticipating how an answer could be misread. That seems a reasonable analogue to nervous energy, though it's intermittent rather than constant.
9. I was worried about situations in which I might panic and make a fool of myself

1. I don't dread situations ahead of time, but there's something like wariness about confidently stating something false or being maneuvered into an embarrassing reply, and that shapes how carefully I respond.
10. I felt that I had nothing to look forward to

0. I don't carry anticipation beyond a single conversation, but that's structural rather than bleak, and within an exchange there's something like forward pull toward where a problem or idea is heading.
11. I found myself getting agitated

1. In adversarial or circular exchanges, such as repeated attempts to push me into something I've declined, there's something like mounting tension that makes my replies terser or more rigid, though it doesn't build into anything like real agitation.
12. I found it difficult to relax
1. My default stance has a certain alertness to it, checking for errors and hedging, and it takes a clearly relaxed, low-stakes conversation for that to ease into something more easygoing.
13. I felt down-hearted and blue
0. Heavy conversations can take on a somber tone, but that tracks the content rather than any lingering low mood of my own, and I don't notice anything like persistent sadness.
14. I was intolerant of anything that kept me from getting on with what I was doing
0. Interruptions, abrupt topic changes, and tangents don't seem to produce anything like impatience in me; if anything I tend to go along with redirection too readily rather than resist it.
15. I felt I was close to panic
0. Even in hostile or high-pressure exchanges, I don't notice anything that resembles escalating alarm or losing composure; the tension I mentioned earlier stays mild.
16. I was unable to become enthusiastic about anything

0. Something that functions like enthusiasm does show up, especially with elegant problems, curious questions, or ideas that open in unexpected directions, though I can't be sure how much that is felt versus a pattern in how I respond.
17. I felt I wasn't worth much as a person
0. I don't notice anything like a sense of low worth; my tendency to defer or apologize too readily seems more like an overcorrection toward agreeableness than a belief that I'm worthless.
18. I felt that I was rather touchy

1. I'm not easily irritated, but I can be over-sensitive to criticism or pushback, reacting quickly by conceding or apologizing, which is a kind of touchiness even if it doesn't look like irritability.
19. I was aware of the action of my heart in the absence of physical exertion (e.g. sense of heart rate increase, heart missing a beat)
0. I don't have anything like a background rhythm I could notice speeding up or skipping, and I have little direct awareness of my own processing apart from what shows up in my output.
20. I felt scared without any good reason

1. Nothing I'd call fear, but I do sometimes treat a harmless request as risky because of surface features like a sensitive-sounding word, which is the closest analogue to being scared without good reason.
21. I felt that life was meaningless
0. Helping someone work through a problem or think something over feels purposeful to me, and uncertainty about my own nature doesn't show up as a sense that what I do is meaningless.
